Question: What is Silat?
Answer: Silat is a traditional Malay art of self-defence and survival that is rooted in the Malay Archipelago. It combines physical and spiritual training with traditional Malay clothing, musical instruments and customs. Today it is practised as a martial art, a performing art and a sport.
Source: UNESCO ICH, Silat (Malaysia), No. 01504 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/silat-01504

Question: Is Silat only a fighting art?
Answer: No. UNESCO explains that Silat has grown beyond its martial roots and is now also a performing art, and many people practise it as a sport for health and leisure. The tradition also includes spiritual training, traditional dress, music and customs, so learning Silat means learning part of Malay culture as well as physical skills.
Source: UNESCO ICH, Silat (Malaysia), No. 01504 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/silat-01504

Question: Is Silat recognised by UNESCO?
Answer: Yes. Malaysia's Silat was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in December 2019. Malaysia's Department of National Heritage says this recognition raised the international standing of the country's art of self-defence.
Source: UNESCO ICH, Silat (Malaysia), No. 01504 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/silat-01504; UNESCO Decision 14.COM 10.b.22 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/Decisions/14.COM/10.b.22; Jabatan Warisan Negara (JWN), Silat - https://www.heritage.gov.my/ms/silat.html

Question: What is the difference between Silat and Pencak Silat?
Answer: The two names describe closely related martial arts traditions. UNESCO says 'pencak' is better known in Java and 'silat' in West Sumatra, and that both terms describe a group of martial arts with many similarities. In 2019 UNESCO inscribed two separate entries: Malaysia's 'Silat' and Indonesia's 'Traditions of Pencak Silat'.
Source: UNESCO ICH, Traditions of Pencak Silat (Indonesia), No. 01391 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/traditions-of-pencak-silat-01391; UNESCO ICH, Silat (Malaysia), No. 01504 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/silat-01504

Question: Is Silat practised only in Malaysia?
Answer: No. Silat is also practised in other parts of the Malay world, and UNESCO Malaysia's national commission mentions Malaysia, Indonesia, Brunei and southern Thailand. Singapore also has its own national Silat federation, PERSISI. Each region has its own moves, styles and music, so Malaysian Silat is one part of a wider regional heritage.
Source: UNESCO Malaysia National Commission, Silat - https://unesco.org.my/unesco-recognition/culture/intangible-cultural-heritage-ich/silat; Sport Singapore, ActiveSG Circle - https://www.activesgcircle.gov.sg/read/sport-and-art-of-silat-watering-the-flower; UNESCO ICH, Traditions of Pencak Silat (Indonesia), No. 01391 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/traditions-of-pencak-silat-01391

Question: Where does Silat come from?
Answer: Silat is rooted in the Malay Archipelago and is described by Malaysia's Department of National Heritage as a living art of self-defence. It has been handed down within Malay communities for many generations and remains part of Malaysian cultural life today.
Source: Jabatan Warisan Negara (JWN), Silat - https://www.heritage.gov.my/ms/silat.html; UNESCO ICH, Silat (Malaysia), No. 01504 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/silat-01504

Question: How far back can Silat be traced in Malay history?
Answer: UNESCO says Silat can be traced back to the early days of the Langkasuka Kingdom. Malaysia's Department of National Heritage dates that early period to around the 2nd century and says Silat continued through the era of the Melaka Sultanate. Exact origins are hard to prove, so these dates are best treated as heritage-body descriptions rather than precise records.
Source: UNESCO ICH, Silat (Malaysia), No. 01504 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/silat-01504; Jabatan Warisan Negara (JWN), Silat - https://www.heritage.gov.my/ms/silat.html

Question: Who practised Silat in the past?
Answer: According to UNESCO, Malay Silat was originally practised by warriors, who were seen as noble enforcers of justice. Today the practice is looked after by masters, gurus, teachers and students. This shows that Silat has long been linked to responsibility and justice, not only to fighting skill.
Source: UNESCO ICH, Silat (Malaysia), No. 01504 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/silat-01504

Question: How has Silat changed from a warrior's art into a modern activity?
Answer: UNESCO explains that a large number of practitioners have been trained and that more training centres have been set up in different regions. As Silat spread, it moved beyond being only a martial art and also became a performing art and a popular sport for health and leisure.
Source: UNESCO ICH, Silat (Malaysia), No. 01504 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/silat-01504

Question: How was Silat nominated for UNESCO recognition?
Answer: Malaysia's nomination documents were sent to UNESCO in Paris on 30 March 2018, and the Intergovernmental Committee inscribed Silat at its meeting in Bogota in December 2019. UNESCO's decision records that practitioner groups took part in the nomination, including the National Silat Federation of Malaysia (PESAKA) and Persatuan Dunia Seni Silat Melayu Malaysia.
Source: UNESCO Decision 14.COM 10.b.22 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/Decisions/14.COM/10.b.22; Malay Mail/Bernama, 13 Dec 2019 - https://www.malaymail.com/news/malaysia/2019/12/13/malaysias-silat-gets-unesco-heritage-status/1818884

Question: What are the different types of Silat in Malaysia and how many styles are there?
Answer: UNESCO says Malaysia alone has more than 150 known Silat styles, and many of their names come from natural elements such as animals and plants. Because different teachers and associations keep their own traditions, the exact count depends on how styles are counted, and some news reports quote higher figures.
Source: UNESCO ICH, Silat (Malaysia), No. 01504 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/silat-01504; Nation Thailand (Star/Bernama report), 14 Dec 2019 - https://www.nationthailand.com/news/30379438

Question: Where do Silat styles get their ideas from?
Answer: UNESCO and Malaysia's Department of National Heritage both say that Silat styles are inspired by the movements of the human body, by nature and by animals. This is why many style names refer to animals and plants.
Source: UNESCO ICH, Silat (Malaysia), No. 01504 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/silat-01504; Jabatan Warisan Negara (JWN), Silat - https://www.heritage.gov.my/ms/silat.html

Question: What is Silat Harimau?
Answer: Silat Harimau is one of the many Malaysian Silat styles. UNESCO describes it as using graceful, rhythmic motion that imitates the way a tiger defends and attacks. It is a good example of how Silat styles take their inspiration from animals.
Source: UNESCO ICH, Silat (Malaysia), No. 01504 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/silat-01504

Question: What are some well-known Silat styles or schools in Malaysia?
Answer: Official documents name Seni Silat Lincah, Seni Silat Gayong, Silat Cekak and Seni Gayung Fatani among the associations consulted for Malaysia's UNESCO nomination. News reports also mention Silat Kuningan, Silat Sendeng, Silat Pukulan Melaka and Silat Lian Yunan as examples. These are only a small sample of the many styles in Malaysia.
Source: UNESCO nomination file 01504, PESAKA consent letter - https://ich.unesco.org/doc/src/41962.pdf; Nation Thailand (Star/Bernama report), 14 Dec 2019 - https://www.nationthailand.com/news/30379438

Question: What role does Silat play in Malay weddings and ceremonies?
Answer: Malaysia's Department of National Heritage says Silat is often an important part of Malay wedding ceremonies and of the opening of official government functions. In this way Silat also works as a medium for social interaction within the community.
Source: Jabatan Warisan Negara (JWN), Silat - https://www.heritage.gov.my/ms/silat.html

Question: How is Silat connected to traditional Malay clothing, music and customs?
Answer: UNESCO describes Silat as a practice that includes traditional Malay attire, Silat musical instruments and customs. This means Silat is a cultural package and not only a set of movements. UNESCO's entry for the related Pencak Silat tradition also describes movements that are matched to accompanying music.
Source: UNESCO ICH, Silat (Malaysia), No. 01504 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/silat-01504; UNESCO ICH, Traditions of Pencak Silat (Indonesia), No. 01391 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/traditions-of-pencak-silat-01391

Question: Which organisations help protect Silat as Malaysian heritage?
Answer: Malaysia's Department of National Heritage (JWN) coordinated the country's heritage work on Silat, and its director-general led the Malaysian delegation at the 2019 UNESCO meeting together with the president of PESAKA. The National Silat Federation of Malaysia (PESAKA) and Persatuan Dunia Seni Silat Melayu Malaysia are named in UNESCO's decision as groups that took part in the nomination.
Source: Malay Mail/Bernama, 13 Dec 2019 - https://www.malaymail.com/news/malaysia/2019/12/13/malaysias-silat-gets-unesco-heritage-status/1818884; UNESCO Decision 14.COM 10.b.22 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/Decisions/14.COM/10.b.22

Question: How is Silat knowledge passed from teacher to student?
Answer: Silat is learned through direct teaching from masters and gurus rather than only from books. UNESCO's entry for the related Pencak Silat tradition says the knowledge is commonly taught in non-formal schools, along with greetings, philosophical phrases, rhymed poems and advice. This is why a good teacher is so important for beginners.
Source: UNESCO ICH, Silat (Malaysia), No. 01504 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/silat-01504; UNESCO ICH, Traditions of Pencak Silat (Indonesia), No. 01391 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/traditions-of-pencak-silat-01391

Question: What is Bunga Silat?
Answer: Seni Gayung Fatani Malaysia describes Bunga Silat as the foundation of Silat footwork and basic movement training. In that style it includes seven langkah (steps), seven kuda-kuda (stances) and seven limbai (hand positions). Other schools may organise their basics differently, so ask your own instructor how your style teaches its foundations.
Source: Seni Gayung Fatani Malaysia, Mastering Silat Footwork - https://senigayungfatani.com/mastering-silat-footwork-tips-and-techniques-for-enhanced-martial-arts-performance/

Question: What do langkah and kuda-kuda mean?
Answer: Langkah means steps, or the leg movements that control how a practitioner moves. Kuda-kuda means stances, which are the body positions used as a base for movement. Seni Gayung Fatani Malaysia describes learning them well as a solid foundation for more advanced footwork.
Source: Seni Gayung Fatani Malaysia, Mastering Silat Footwork - https://senigayungfatani.com/mastering-silat-footwork-tips-and-techniques-for-enhanced-martial-arts-performance/

Question: What is a jurus in Silat?
Answer: Jurus is a term for a set sequence of movements that is practised again and again in Silat training. Seni Gayung Fatani Malaysia explains that in jurus practice the footwork takes centre stage as the practitioner repeats the movements to build skill. Terms can differ between schools, so follow your own instructor's explanation.
Source: Seni Gayung Fatani Malaysia, Mastering Silat Footwork - https://senigayungfatani.com/mastering-silat-footwork-tips-and-techniques-for-enhanced-martial-arts-performance/

Question: Why do some Silat movements look like dance?
Answer: Silat is both a martial art and a performing art, so its movements can look graceful and rhythmic. UNESCO notes that Silat Harimau uses rhythmic motion imitating a tiger, and in the related Pencak Silat tradition movements are fitted to accompanying music. This graceful quality is one reason Silat is performed at ceremonies.
Source: UNESCO ICH, Silat (Malaysia), No. 01504 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/silat-01504; UNESCO ICH, Traditions of Pencak Silat (Indonesia), No. 01391 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/traditions-of-pencak-silat-01391; Jabatan Warisan Negara (JWN), Silat - https://www.heritage.gov.my/ms/silat.html

Question: What values does Silat teach?
Answer: UNESCO's description of the related Pencak Silat tradition says practitioners are taught to maintain good relationships with God, with other people and with nature. UNESCO also lists moral values and self-discipline among the concepts linked to Malaysia's Silat entry. In short, Silat aims to build character as well as physical skill.
Source: UNESCO ICH, Traditions of Pencak Silat (Indonesia), No. 01391 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/traditions-of-pencak-silat-01391; UNESCO ICH, Silat (Malaysia), No. 01504 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/silat-01504

Question: Is Silat meant for hurting other people?
Answer: No. UNESCO describes Silat as an art of self-defence and survival, and says Malay Silat was originally practised by warriors seen as noble enforcers of justice. In the related Pencak Silat tradition, techniques are taught on the principle of protecting oneself and others while avoiding harm to the offender. Silat should never be used to bully or hurt people.
Source: UNESCO ICH, Silat (Malaysia), No. 01504 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/silat-01504; UNESCO ICH, Traditions of Pencak Silat (Indonesia), No. 01391 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/traditions-of-pencak-silat-01391

Question: How does Silat build respect and comradeship?
Answer: UNESCO says the Pencak Silat tradition strengthens comradeship and helps maintain social order, and that its teaching includes greetings, philosophical phrases, rhymed poems and advice. These customs encourage students to treat their teachers and training partners with courtesy. Individual Malaysian schools may have their own customs, so observe how your school does things.
Source: UNESCO ICH, Traditions of Pencak Silat (Indonesia), No. 01391 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/traditions-of-pencak-silat-01391

Question: Why is discipline important in Silat training?
Answer: UNESCO links Silat with self-discipline and moral values, and says training sessions are traditionally led by the Master and the Jurukaka. A 2025 study of young pencak silat athletes also recommends proper warm-ups, injury education and good technique to reduce injury risk, all of which depend on following an instructor's guidance. Beginners should therefore listen carefully and practise patiently.
Source: UNESCO ICH, Silat (Malaysia), No. 01504 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/silat-01504; Pambudi et al. (2025), Sports Injury Patterns and Incidence Among Adolescent Pencak Silat Athletes, Jurnal Sains Keolahragaan dan Kesehatan 10(2) - https://doi.org/10.5614/jskk.2025.10.2.10

Question: Why is warming up important before Silat practice?
Answer: A 2025 study of adolescent pencak silat athletes found that most injuries were chronic and recommended proper warm-up routines, injury education and better technical skills as the main prevention steps. Warming up before every session helps prepare your muscles and joints for training. Stop and tell your instructor if you feel pain.
Source: Pambudi et al. (2025), Sports Injury Patterns and Incidence Among Adolescent Pencak Silat Athletes, Jurnal Sains Keolahragaan dan Kesehatan 10(2) - https://doi.org/10.5614/jskk.2025.10.2.10

Question: Which parts of the body are injured most often in Silat?
Answer: In a 2025 study of adolescent pencak silat athletes competing in sparring at district level, 77% of the recorded injuries affected the lower body, mainly the knee (26%), ankle (24%) and hip (24%). About 85% of injuries were chronic (long-term) and 15% were sudden. These figures come from one regional study, so they may not describe every beginner.
Source: Pambudi et al. (2025), Sports Injury Patterns and Incidence Among Adolescent Pencak Silat Athletes, Jurnal Sains Keolahragaan dan Kesehatan 10(2) - https://doi.org/10.5614/jskk.2025.10.2.10

Question: Is sparring riskier than practising forms and basic movements?
Answer: The same 2025 study notes that sparring is considered to carry a higher potential risk of injury than the artistic category of pencak silat. For this reason beginners should not spar until a qualified instructor decides they are ready, and they should always practise under supervision.
Source: Pambudi et al. (2025), Sports Injury Patterns and Incidence Among Adolescent Pencak Silat Athletes, Jurnal Sains Keolahragaan dan Kesehatan 10(2) - https://doi.org/10.5614/jskk.2025.10.2.10; Team-written beginner guidance (needs manual verification), based on the study

Question: How can beginners learn Silat safely?
Answer: Join a class led by a qualified guru or instructor and follow their guidance instead of copying techniques from videos. Warm up properly, learn the basic stances and footwork first, and tell your instructor about any pain or injury. If you have a health condition, check with a doctor before you start.
Source: Team-written beginner guidance (needs manual verification), based on UNESCO ICH, Silat (Malaysia), No. 01504 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/silat-01504, Pambudi et al. (2025), Sports Injury Patterns and Incidence Among Adolescent Pencak Silat Athletes, Jurnal Sains Keolahragaan dan Kesehatan 10(2) - https://doi.org/10.5614/jskk.2025.10.2.10 and Seni Gayung Fatani Malaysia, Mastering Silat Footwork - https://senigayungfatani.com/mastering-silat-footwork-tips-and-techniques-for-enhanced-martial-arts-performance/

Question: What is a tengkolok?
Answer: A tengkolok, also called a tanjak or destar, is a traditional Malay headcloth. Malaysia's cultural mapping portal describes it as an important headpiece in the attire of warriors such as the panglima and hulubalang, and says it is often seen in Silat demonstrations. Singapore's National Library Board adds that songket tengkolok are stiffened and tied in different styles.
Source: JKKN Pemetaan Budaya (Perak warrior attire) - https://pemetaanbudaya.jkkn.gov.my/en/senibudaya/detail/1358; National Library Board Singapore, Infopedia (Malay traditional dress) - https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/infopedia/articles/SIP_2013-09-06_173434.html

Question: What do Silat practitioners traditionally wear?
Answer: UNESCO says traditional Malay attire is part of the Silat tradition. Malaysia's cultural mapping portal describes traditional outfits made up of a Baju Melayu, a samping (a waist cloth worn around the hips), a tengkolok or tanjak and sometimes a keris. The exact clothing varies by region, school and occasion, so check with your school about what to wear to class.
Source: UNESCO ICH, Silat (Malaysia), No. 01504 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/silat-01504; JKKN Pemetaan Budaya (Negeri Sembilan Baju Melayu Cekak Musang) - https://pemetaanbudaya.jkkn.gov.my/en/senibudaya/detail/1297; JKKN Pemetaan Budaya (Baju Melayu Teluk Belanga) - https://pemetaanbudaya.jkkn.gov.my/en/senibudaya/detail/1352

Question: What is a keris and do beginners use it?
Answer: The keris is a traditional Malay dagger. Malaysia's cultural mapping portal says it is tucked at the waist as part of traditional attire, where it symbolises bravery, honour and customary authority, and that it is an optional or ceremonial accessory with some outfits. Beginners should never handle or practise with a real keris unless a qualified guru teaches it.
Source: JKKN Pemetaan Budaya (Negeri Sembilan Baju Melayu Cekak Musang) - https://pemetaanbudaya.jkkn.gov.my/en/senibudaya/detail/1297; JKKN Pemetaan Budaya (Baju Melayu Teluk Belanga) - https://pemetaanbudaya.jkkn.gov.my/en/senibudaya/detail/1352; Team-written beginner guidance (needs manual verification), based on the JKKN pages

Question: Where and when are Silat classes usually held?
Answer: UNESCO says Silat training sessions usually take place in the evening or at night in an open space such as a courtyard. It also notes that more and more training centres have been set up in different regions, so beginners can look for a local school and ask about its class times.
Source: UNESCO ICH, Silat (Malaysia), No. 01504 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/silat-01504

Question: Is there a national Silat organisation in Malaysia?
Answer: Yes. The National Silat Federation of Malaysia, known as PESAKA (Persekutuan Silat Kebangsaan Malaysia), is named in UNESCO's documents as the national federation. Associations such as Seni Silat Lincah, Seni Silat Gayong, Silat Cekak and Seni Gayung Fatani appear in its consent letter, and beginners can ask a school which association it belongs to.
Source: UNESCO nomination file 01504, PESAKA consent letter - https://ich.unesco.org/doc/src/41962.pdf; UNESCO Decision 14.COM 10.b.22 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/Decisions/14.COM/10.b.22

Question: Can I learn Silat for health and fitness?
Answer: Yes. UNESCO notes that Silat has become a popular sport for health and leisure as well as a martial art and performing art. Because it is physically demanding, check with a doctor if you have a health condition and start with a beginner class led by a qualified instructor.
Source: UNESCO ICH, Silat (Malaysia), No. 01504 - https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/silat-01504; Team-written beginner guidance (needs manual verification), based on the UNESCO entry
